summary: Internet mail was limited to 7-bit ASCII, and MIME added 8-bit body support and encoded-words for some header values. This RFC permits Unicode directly in email headers, including addresses, for full internationalization.

plainLanguage.summary: Email header lines used to hold only plain Latin letters. RFC 6532 lets them hold any letter from any writing system, in the sender's address as well as in the subject line. The message stores those letters as UTF-8 text instead of packing them into a coded form, and the whole path from sender to receiver has to carry the bytes unchanged.

subtitle: Lets email headers and addresses carry Unicode text directly, with no encoded-word tricks.

tldr.problem: Email header lines, including the addresses, could hold only plain 7-bit ASCII characters, so a sender could not write a name in its own script.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the header grammar of RFC 5322 so UTF-8 may appear in most header field values and in addresses, and it registers a new media type, message/global, for such messages.
tldr.outcome: The RFC obsoletes RFC 5335 and updates a MIME rule about transfer encodings. Sending such mail over SMTP requires the SMTPUTF8 extension of RFC 6531.

today: RFC 6532 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. It obsoletes RFC 5335 and updates RFC 2045, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It is meant to be used with the SMTPUTF8 extension defined in RFC 6531.

sections.title: Why Header Text Was Limited
sections.content:
Internet mail separates a message from its transport and splits the message into a header and a body. The header holds strings that people read, such as the sender, the recipients and the subject. Those strings were limited to 7-bit ASCII. MIME later added support for other character sets in body parts, and gave header fields a coded form called an encoded-word, but only in a limited number of header positions.

RFC 6532 removes that limit for most header values and for mail addresses. The RFC argues that globalized mail needs the much larger set of characters Unicode provides, that encoded-words bring inefficiency and significant opportunities for processing errors, and that native support for UTF-8 is now available on most systems.

The design assumes native, end-to-end support for UTF-8, which depends on an 8-bit-clean environment assured by the transport system. Support for crossing legacy 7-bit infrastructure, and for processing by 7-bit receivers, requires additional mechanisms that these specifications do not provide. The document is a revision of and replacement for RFC 5335.
sections.plainLanguage: Header lines such as the subject and the sender's address used to hold only plain Latin letters. This RFC lets them hold any letter from any writing system. That only works when the whole path from sender to receiver can carry those bytes without changing them.

sections.title: Extending the Header Grammar
sections.content:
The header definition in RFC 5322 is extended by adding the rule UTF8-non-ascii to six productions: VCHAR, ctext, atext, qtext, text and dtext. Because text covers the body as well, that rule upgrades the body to UTF-8 too. Rules that are not mentioned stay as they are in RFC 5322.

The changes let UTF-8 appear in four kinds of place: unstructured text, used in header fields such as Subject: and Content-description:; any construct that uses atoms, including the local parts of addresses and Message-IDs, and the addresses in the for clauses of Received: fields; quoted strings; and domains.

Header field names do not change. The bodies of header fields may contain Unicode characters, but the names themselves must consist of ASCII characters only. Messages in this format also require the SMTPUTF8 extension of RFC 6531 to be transferred over SMTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for writing header lines now accept letters from any writing system, in plain text, in addresses and in quoted text. The names of the fields, such as To and Subject, still have to use plain Latin letters.

sections.title: UTF-8 Syntax and Normalization
sections.content:
The RFC defines the octets of a non-ASCII character with the ABNF rules of RFC 3629 and calls the resulting construct UTF8-non-ascii. A non-ASCII string is a UTF-8 string when it appears in a header field value that contains at least one such construct. A plain ASCII string stays fully compatible with RFC 5321 and RFC 5322.

Because Unicode offers more than one way to write the same or a similar character, the RFC points to the discussion in RFC 5198 and says that normalization form NFC SHOULD be used. The form NFKC SHOULD NOT be used, because it may lose information that is needed to correctly spell some names in unusual circumstances. The reason is stated plainly: many mailbox local parts reflect personal names, so the goal of letting people spell their names correctly applies to mailboxes as well.

Implementers of Message-ID generation algorithms MAY prefer to restrain their output to ASCII. That helps when constructing In-reply-to: and References: header fields in mailing-list threads where some senders use internationalized addresses and others do not.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters can be written on a computer in more than one way. The RFC asks senders to use the standard form, NFC, so that the same name always looks and compares the same. It warns against a more aggressive form because that form can change how a name is spelled.

sections.title: Effects on Line Length Limits
sections.content:
Section 2.1.1 of RFC 5322 limits lines to 998 characters and recommends that lines be restricted to only 78 characters. This specification changes the first limit to 998 octets. In ASCII, octets and characters are effectively the same thing, but that is not true in UTF-8.

The 78-character limit remains defined in terms of characters rather than octets, because it is intended to address display width issues, not line-length issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The long line limit used to count characters. It now counts bytes, because one character can take several bytes in UTF-8. The shorter recommended line length still counts characters, since it is about how wide a line looks.

sections.title: Encoded-Words and Transfer Encodings
sections.content:
The MIME encoded-word facility of RFC 2047 can place non-ASCII text in a header field, but only in a subset of the places this extension allows, and it is substantially more complex because it allows arbitrary character sets. Encoded-words SHOULD NOT be used when generating header fields for messages that use this extension. Agents MAY convert encoded-word use to direct use of UTF-8 when they incorporate material from another message. Processors that elect to decode encoded-words MUST NOT generate syntactically invalid fields, because the decoded result in UTF-8 may be invalid.

The specification also updates Section 6.4 of RFC 2045. That section prohibits applying a content-transfer-encoding to any subtype of message/. The prohibition is relaxed so that newly defined MIME types may permit one, and so that message/global may carry one.

Normally, transfer of message/global is done in 8-bit-clean channels and body parts have identity encodings, meaning no decoding is necessary. But when a message containing a message/global is downgraded from 8-bit to 7-bit as described in RFC 6152, an encoding might have to be applied to the message. If the message travels several times between a 7-bit environment and one implementing these extensions, multiple levels of encoding may occur. The RFC expects this to be rarely seen in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The older trick of packing unusual letters into a coded form is now discouraged, because the same text can be stored as UTF-8 instead. One case remains: mail that has to cross a path which cannot carry those bytes may need an extra encoding layer.

sections.title: The message/global Media Type
sections.content:
The RFC registers a new media type, message/global, for messages in this format. A message is a message/global message if it contains 8-bit UTF-8 header values as specified in the document, or if it contains 8-bit UTF-8 values in the header fields of body parts. The content of a message/global part is otherwise identical to that of a message/rfc822 part.

Internationalized messages in this format MUST only be transmitted as authorized by RFC 6531 or within a non-SMTP environment that supports such messages. If such an object is sent to a 7-bit-only system, it MUST have an appropriate content-transfer-encoding applied. A system compliant with MIME that does not recognize message/global is supposed to treat it as application/octet-stream.

The registration names the type message and the subtype global, with no required or optional parameters. Any content-transfer-encoding is permitted, and the 8-bit or binary encodings are recommended where permitted. The suggested file extension is .u8msg and the suggested Macintosh uniform type identifier is public.utf8-email-message.
sections.plainLanguage: A new label, message/global, marks a message that uses Unicode in its header lines. It says the same thing as message/rfc822, except that the text may use any writing system.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because UTF-8 often requires several octets to encode a single character, header field values and mail addresses can become longer. Each line of characters MUST be no more than 998 octets, excluding the CRLF. Mail Delivery Agent processes that parse, store or handle email addresses or local parts must take extra care not to overflow buffers, truncate addresses or exceed storage allotments, and must use the entire lengths of addresses when comparing them.

There are many ways to use UTF-8 to represent something equivalent or similar to a particular displayed character or group of characters. The security considerations in RFC 3629 describe the problems this can cause, and the normalization process described earlier is recommended to minimize them.

The security impact of UTF-8 headers on email signature systems such as DKIM, S/MIME and OpenPGP is discussed in Section 14 of RFC 6530. A user with both a non-ASCII and an ASCII mailbox address might need a certificate that carries both addresses as identities. PKIX and OpenPGP already support multiple email addresses in one certificate, but the RFC notes possible user-interface issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Letters from other writing systems can take more bytes than plain ones, so programs that store addresses must check that longer values do not overflow. Characters that look the same can also be written in different ways, which is why the standard form is recommended.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has updated the registration of the message/global MIME type using the registration form contained in Section 3.7 of the document.

The registration records the intended usage as COMMON and the restrictions on usage: this is a structured media type that embeds other MIME media types, and an 8-bit or binary content-transfer-encoding SHOULD be used unless the media type is sent over a 7-bit-only transport. It lists the applications that use the type as SMTP servers and email clients that support multipart/report generation or parsing, and email clients that forward messages with internationalized headers as attachments.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority to record the new message/global label in the list of media types, so that senders and receivers agree on what it means.

viz.caption: THE SIX GRAMMAR RULES EXTENDED FOR UTF-8 (RFC 6532 SECTION 3.2)

data.title: Grammar extensions
data.code:
VCHAR   =/  UTF8-non-ascii

ctext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii

atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii

qtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii

text    =/  UTF8-non-ascii
                  ; note that this upgrades the body to UTF-8

dtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii

viz.caption: PLACES WHERE UTF-8 MAY NOW APPEAR

items.title: Unstructured text
items.text: Header fields such as Subject and Content-description.

items.title: Atoms
items.text: Local parts of addresses, Message-IDs, and the for clause of Received.

items.title: Quoted strings
items.text: Text inside quotation marks in a header value.

items.title: Domains
items.text: The domain part of an address.
